about: Test vectors for the synced notebook's end-to-end encryption (STUDY-DESK-ENCRYPTION.md), made by the code the website ships (src/lib/desk-crypto.mjs). The website and both apps run this file in their own tests. Every case says what it tests in `why`, what the client starts from in `given`, and what it must arrive at in `expected`: values, or `refused` with the reason. Every random input is fixed and written here, and every private key comes with its public key (`d` beside `public`). These are test values, made from labels by SHA-256; none is a real key.
conventions: Byte strings are lowercase hex. The exceptions are inside text the spec itself defines: a `plaintext` or `text` (JSON as it is sealed) carries its byte strings in base64url, as do a MAC's `macInput` and the passkey responses under `prf`.

A `plaintext` or `text` is JSON given as a string; the bytes are its UTF-8. A client that seals must seal those bytes to reproduce a ciphertext here. Its own serializer may order keys or write numbers differently, so what it makes itself it checks by opening it again.
A sealed value is its `nonce` (12 bytes) and its `ciphertext`, which ends with the 16-byte tag. A row's are called `nonce` and `ct`, as the service's row has them.
An AAD is given as text (`aad`), with its line feeds, and for some cases as bytes too (`aadHex`).
A keyring, where it is an expected value, is `{ notebook, current, keys: [{ kid, key }] }` with the keys in hex, newest first. Compare by kid, not by order.

`refused` is one of the words under `refusals`. A client need not use the words, but it must refuse every case marked so, and where the spec treats two refusals differently (`aside`, a holder's `check`), it must tell them apart.
HPKE and ECDSA cases run in the opening and the verifying direction. The sender's one-use key (`ephemeral`) and the signing number are given for a client that can fix them.
Times are the format's: UTC with Z. Ids are UUIDs in lowercase with hyphens.

seal.about: Sealing a record: pad its serialized bytes, make the AAD from the plain fields, and seal with AES-256-GCM under the record key of the notebook key `kid`. `plaintext` is the record's JSON as text; the bytes sealed are its UTF-8. A client seals these exact bytes to reproduce `row.ct`; what it makes from its own serializer differs and is checked by opening it again. `aad` is the AAD as text and `aadHex` its bytes: lines lit-row/1, the kid in decimal, id, modified, and deletedAt, where a record that isn't trash has an empty last line, so its AAD ends with a line feed. A `row` is the row of the spec's "A record on the service" without `rev`, with `nonce` and `ct` in hex here (the service carries them in base64url), and `ct` ends with the 16-byte tag.

openRefused.about: Rows that must not be accepted, each with one thing wrong. `aside: true` (an unknown `v`, or a `kid` the device doesn't hold) means keep the row aside and fetch the keyring; every other refusal means skip the row, keep the device's own copy, and report it. No refusal ever deletes anything. The checks run in this order: the row's version, its kid, its own fields, the ciphertext's length, the seal, the JSON, and last the record's fields against the plain ones.

padding.about: A serialized record is padded with spaces (0x20) to the next multiple of 256 bytes; a length already a multiple of 256 takes none. `ciphertext` is the padded length plus the 16-byte tag. A record is never empty and never more than 1,048,576 bytes.

keyring.about: `parse` is the keyring's own checks, on the JSON a sealed keyring opens to: `lit` and `v` known (`version`), the kids exactly the whole numbers from 1 to `current`, each once (`kids`), every key 32 bytes of base64url (`keySize`). `accept` is what a device that already holds a keyring (`held`: its notebook, the highest `current` it has accepted, and its keys) asks of one taken from the service: the same notebook (`notebook`), a `current` no lower than the highest accepted (`backward`), and every key it holds with the same bytes (`keyChanged`). A keyring that drops a held key is either malformed or lower, so it is refused by `parse` or as `backward`.

hpkeOpen.about: HPKE (RFC 9180) in base mode, single-shot, with DHKEM(P-256, HKDF-SHA256), HKDF-SHA256, and AES-256-GCM (0x0010, 0x0001, 0x0002): the `info` is the ASCII bytes of lit-notebook/1 keyring and the AAD is empty. The cases run in the opening direction, since a platform's HPKE makes its own sender key: given the recipient's key pair, `enc`, and the ciphertext, the client opens the keyring. `sharedSecret`, `key`, and `baseNonce` are the values along the way, for a client that writes HPKE by hand; the nonce used is the base nonce (sequence number 0). `sender.ephemeral` is the sender's one-use key pair, for a client that can fix it and wants to reproduce the sealing too. Each client also checks that what it seals, it opens.

prf.about: The fixed input a passkey's PRF is evaluated at, in each form a client meets it, and what leaves the device. `bytes` is the 18 ASCII bytes given as the extension's first value (`eval.first`); `base64url` is how a request's JSON carries them (Android's Credential Manager); `hashed` is what the platform sends the passkey, SHA-256 of the ASCII bytes of WebAuthn PRF, one zero byte, and the input. `responses` are passkey responses in the JSON form (made-up bytes, in base64url as that form has them): before a response goes to the service, `clientExtensionResults.prf.results` is removed and nothing else is, and the service refuses a response that still has it.

passkeyHolder.about: The passkey key is HKDF(the PRF's 32 bytes, lit-notebook/1 passkey, 32 bytes). `answered` is the credential id of the passkey that just answered. `service` is what the service hands a device that asks to come in through the holder: its kind, id, and the notebook's id in plain, the sealed record (AES-256-GCM under the secret's key, with the AAD lines lit-holder/1, the kind, and the id), and the keyring sealed to the holder's public key with HPKE. The four checks run in order and stop at the first failure; a refusal's `check` says which: 1, the record opens; 2, the record is what it should be; 3, the sealed keyring opens with the record's private key and passes the keyring's own checks; 4, the keyring names the record's notebook and holds the anchor's key with the same bytes. `plaintext` is the record's JSON, with its byte strings in base64url as the spec says; `holderKey` is the holder's key pair in hex.

recoveryHolder.about: The code key is HKDF(the code's 15 bytes, lit-notebook/1 recovery, 32 bytes). `typed` is the code as the reader types it. `service` is what the service hands a device that asks to come in through the holder: its kind, id, and the notebook's id in plain, the sealed record (AES-256-GCM under the secret's key, with the AAD lines lit-holder/1, the kind, and the id), and the keyring sealed to the holder's public key with HPKE. The four checks run in order and stop at the first failure; a refusal's `check` says which: 1, the record opens; 2, the record is what it should be; 3, the sealed keyring opens with the record's private key and passes the keyring's own checks; 4, the keyring names the record's notebook and holds the anchor's key with the same bytes. `plaintext` is the record's JSON, with its byte strings in base64url as the spec says; `holderKey` is the holder's key pair in hex.

approval.about: Adding a device by approval. Both devices make the approval's id (HKDF of the code's 10 bytes with lit-notebook/1 approve-id, 16 bytes, written as 32 lowercase hex characters) and its MAC key (HKDF with lit-notebook/1 approve-mac, 32 bytes). Each MAC is HMAC-SHA-256 over lines, given here as `macInput` (text) with the keys and ciphertexts in base64url, as the MAC takes them. The grant's keyring is sealed with HPKE as in `hpkeOpen`, and its card is the new device's card, written by the approving device: the model as its name, and both public keys from the request. The new device checks, in order: the grant's MAC (`mac`); that the keyring opens and passes its own checks; that its `current` is the grant's kid (`grantKid`); and that the card opens for its own id under that key and names both of its public keys (`card`).

signingKey.about: The signing key, reserved: every device makes one (P-256, for ECDSA with SHA-256) and carries its public half in its card as `sign`, and nothing checks a signature in version 1. These cases are for the day something does. A signature is the 64 bytes r ‖ s (WebCrypto's output and CryptoKit's rawRepresentation); `der` is the same signature as Android's Signature gives it, and each form converts to the other. ECDSA picks a fresh number for every signature, so the cases run in the verifying direction; `signer.number` is the number these were made with, for a client that can fix it. Each client also checks that what it signs, it verifies.

point.about: A public key is the 65-byte uncompressed point, 04 ‖ x ‖ y, with x and y each less than the field's size and y² = x³ − 3x + b. Every public key a client is given, and HPKE's `enc`, is checked before it is used; anything else is refused.

walkthrough.about: One notebook from its first device to a recovery, every value along the way. Each step's `given` holds what the step starts from and every fixed random input it uses (nonces, and the sender key of each HPKE seal as `ephemerals`); `expected` holds what a client following the spec arrives at. A sealed card or holder record is given as its `plaintext` (the JSON as text), its `aad` (as text), its `nonce`, and its `ciphertext`; a sealed keyring as its `enc` and `ciphertext`, with the sender's key for a client that can fix it. A client that can't fix a sender key or reproduce another client's JSON byte for byte follows the walkthrough in the opening direction: every `ciphertext` here must open to the plaintext beside it.

steps.what: The first device (A) sets up under “follows my account”: it makes the notebook's id and first key, its own keys and card, and a passkey holder, and sends the service the proof's hash, its card, the holder, and a keyring sealed to itself and to the holder.
A pushes its notebook, each record sealed under the record key of kid 1.

A second device (B) joins by passkey. The passkey gives it the same 32 bytes; it makes the passkey key, opens the holder's record, runs the four checks, and has the keyring. It writes its own card, seals the keyring to its own device key, proves the key, and opens the rows.

records.body: Who is the whole world here?

steps.what: A third device (C) is approved by B. C shows a code; both make the approval's id and MAC key from it; C posts its request; B checks the request's MAC and grants, sealing its keyring to C's key and writing C's card; C checks the grant, keeps the keyring, and proves the key.

The first device (A) is removed, from C. C makes the next notebook key and a keyring with it as current, seals that keyring to B, to itself, and to the passkey holder (never to A), seals every kept card again under the new key, sends the new proof's hash, and seals every record again under the new key. B fetches its new sealed keyring and accepts it, since it holds every key B already has. A, which still has the old keyring, can't open the new rows.

The reader switches to “this device only,” from C. The notebook gets a third key, the passkey holder is removed and gets no keyring, and since the reader has no recovery code, one is made in the same step: a recovery holder, anchored to the new key. Whoever still has the passkey has, at most, the keyring it was last given, which holds no key that opens anything sealed from now on.

The reader has lost every device, and signs in on a fourth (D) with the recovery code, typed in lowercase with spaces. D makes the code key, opens the recovery holder's record, runs the four checks, and has the keyring; it writes its card, seals the keyring to itself, proves the key, and opens the rows.

records.body: Who is the whole world here?

steps.what: Forgeries. The service has seen C's public key (in its approval request), so it can seal a keyring of its own to C; and anyone who learned the recovery holder's public key can seal one to it. Neither has ever held a notebook key. C refuses the first because it changes keys C holds, C refuses its own old keyring handed back because it goes backward, and a device coming in by code refuses the last because it lacks the anchor's key.
